parts:
Hi guys, for my master's thesis, I have to do a SEM.


I've got longitudinal data from 150 babies and their mothers at 3 time points.


My first aim is to investigate how maternal cognitions (measured by 3 questionnaire scales anger, doubt and limit setting), maternal sleep (measured by 3 questionnaire items, 2 items for waking up and 1 for sleep duration) and the baby's sleep (measured by motion detection, the variables are nightwakings, sleep duration day and total sleep duration) is connected at each time point, supposing that there's a direct and indirect effect of maternal cognitions on baby's sleep (indirectly over maternal sleep). Also, I'd like to observe if maternal cognitons and sleep at time points 1 and 2 can predict baby's sleep at time points 2 and 3.

The idea is, if mothers have high scores in the cognition scales, their babys are likely to wake up more and sleep more during the day and less during the night.


My second aim is to observe if stress during pregnancy (measured by a stress questionnaire) can predict baby's sleep (nightwakings, sleep duration day, total sleep duration and co-sleeping) at time points 1, 2 and 3.

I've tried to model each time point separately and the predictions as well in a different model, bc it didn't work with all time points and predictions in one model, maybe bc it's too much to handle for lavaan with such a small sample? However, when I try to fit the models, I always get the following warning message, also when I try to fit the predictions and stress during pregnancy in separate models:


lavaan WARNING: the optimizer warns that a solution has NOT been found!


Here's my R-Code:

'

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: SEM longitudinal data; warning message solution not found
parts: Does anyone know what I am doing wrong or have suggestions how I can handle this better?

Your model is probably so wrong that it can't possibly account for the data.  I'm guessing the problem is that your common factors are not actually common factors.  CFA is not about mere dimension-reduction, it is postulating a single common cause of a set of indicators.  For example, if SleepBaby_T1 goes up by 1 unit, the T1_Nightwakings_z, T1_SleepDurationDay_z, and T1_SleepDurationWhole_z simultaneously increase by their factor loadings.  Does this make sense, or is it more sensible that these indicators affect each other directly?

You can try fitting one-factor models to each factor to see where the convergence issue lies.  You can also check correlation matrices among a set of indicators you think go together, to see if the indicators are even correlated enough (at least 0.3 if convergence is to be probable, but at least 0.5 for it to be worth your time).

Also, do not fit models to z scores.  It biases your tests.  You can request a standardizedSolution(), but always analyze raw data. 

Ultimately, your model is too big for your sample, so I would recommend focusing on one small part at a time.  You can also ask for help on the more general SEM forum SEMNET:

http://www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Re: SEM longitudinal data; warning message solution not found
parts: You can solve that problem by dividing (ormultipying) some of your observed variables by some constant, like a suitable power of 10. Dividing by a constant does not complicate sttistical distributions, like dividing by a sample-based quantity does. Look at the variances of your observed variables, and remember that dividing the raw score by X divides the variance by X squared.

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: SEM longitudinal data; warning message solution not found
parts: Can you tell me how exactly I can do this in R?

If your data.frame is called "mydata", it is as simple as adding another variable to that data.frame.  This command divides every value in the variable "T1_SleepDurationDay" by 10, storing those rescaled values in a new variable "T1_SleepDurationDay10"

mydata$T1_SleepDurationDay10 <- mydata$T1_SleepDurationDay / 10

Now, each 1-unit change in "T1_SleepDurationDay10" is interpreted as "per 10 units" (e.g., per 10 hours).

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: SEM longitudinal data; warning message solution not found
parts: what does it mean exactly?

It means what it says: one of your (residual) variances is negative:

Variances:
                   Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)
   .SleepBaby_T3     -0.168    0.189   -0.890    0.374

The estimate is smaller than its SE, so the CI would include positive values.  Perhaps it's just an artifact of sampling error, but perhaps your model is wrong for the reasons I explained before.  SleepBaby_T3 does not have a pattern of loadings that suggests there is a common cause at play.  Your SleepBaby_T3 indicators seem like they are definitionally related rather than having a common cause (i.e., isn't sleep duration during the day part of the "whole" sleep duration? and wouldn't they both necessarily be shorter if there are more night wakings?).

Look at the pattern of correlations among items with each construct, and compare those to the correlations of items between the 2 constructs.

cov2cor(lavInspect(fit3, "sampstat")$cov)

Are there any negative correlations among indicators that are supposed to have a common cause/factor?  Are there any stronger correlations between factors than the ones within factors?  

And check which relationships your model fails to reproduce:

lavResiduals(fit3)

Does it look like some indicators may have stronger direct effects on other indicators than your latent regression allows for?

Again, factor analysis is not about dimension reduction; it is a theoretical model of common latent causes of observable variables.  If this model doesn't hold for your "indicators", then you might be better off treating those 3 indicators as separate outcomes (or causes... wouldn't a mother's anger and doubt be affected by how much the baby sleeps or how often it wakes her up?).

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
